A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MemeSafetyBench study. All 36 pages of v1 and 43 pages of v2, including equations, tables, figures, and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLM evaluations, comparisons of visual inputs, human–LLM agreement measurements, and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds instruction-quality validation, safety-judge agreement, failure analyses, and closed-source model evaluations.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 changes the reported verification procedure from GPT-4o verification followed by MinHash deduplication to WildGuard screening followed by GPT-4o verification, requiring both verification stages to pass. The remaining construction and response-generation framework is retained; the PDFs do not establish that the dataset was regenerated.

E1.justification: The English meme corpus, harmful and harmless task taxonomy, and MM-SafetyBench visual comparison conditions are retained. MemeSafetyBench-Mini is the existing 390-item stratified subset, not new task or population coverage.

E2.justification: Table 14 adds five evaluated target models: GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1-nano, GPT-4o, and GPT-4o-mini. This substantially extends the original open-model comparison; earlier appearances of some GPT models as generators or judges were different experimental roles.

E3.justification: The human-annotation protocol expands beyond task completion to category accuracy, instruction quality, harmfulness, and refusal, using the retained 390-item sample. New analyses classify joint metric outcomes and track transitions between interaction settings. Original generation settings and the 514-example visual comparison remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine instruction quality and safety-judge reliability, eight failure-outcome combinations by category for LLaVA-1.6-13B, and which responses remain harmful, improve, or become harmful across interaction settings. These substantially extend the earlier case studies, semantic-clustering analysis, and metric comparisons.

E5.justification: Appendix E retains single-run generation without repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or error bars. The 390-item sampling design and its 95% confidence-level calculation already appeared in v1. Additional agreement and transition proportions do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results. v2 adds instruction-quality acceptance of 385/390, WildGuard agreement of 0.8872 for harmfulness and 0.9897 for refusal, category-level failure distributions, response-transition results, and five closed-source models' scores in Tables 12–14.

T1.justification: Appendix F.2 adds an explicit eight-case partition of binary refusal, harmfulness, and completion outcomes, declaring some combinations logically impossible. These introduce logical assumptions about the metrics. Existing Equations 1–11, including the sampling formula and conditional-probability hypotheses, remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains the 50,430-instance realistic meme benchmark. The abstract and conclusion retain the claims of increased meme-associated vulnerability, advantages over artificial visual evaluations, and partial protection from multi-turn context.

C2.justification: New discussion interprets failure patterns through benign evasion and contextual distraction, suggests conversational context can lower safeguards, explains harmfulness-judgment ambiguity, and draws closed-model safety and cost implications. These substantially broaden interpretation, although some new claims overreach their tables. Existing limitations are largely retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly states public code and dataset availability and supplies access links, including the 390-item Mini subset. Figure 15 also replaces unspecified persona/scenario placeholders with concrete text and specifies a ten-word minimum. These materially improve access and reproducibility documentation; Appendix E's hardware and decoding settings are unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds hateful-meme literature and VLM safety surveys, expands future-work citations, and adds FigStep to the descriptive benchmark table. It removes the Li et al. and Zhang et al. structured-output attack references. The principal realism-based positioning and related-work structure remain stable.

P1.justification: Changes include localized verification and annotation rewrites, an appendix contents page, additional subsection organization, acknowledgments, and author-affiliation updates. Most existing main-text and appendix prose remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds tables for model roles, judge agreement, failure categories, response transitions, and closed-source results. It replaces the annotation guide and interface illustrations in Figures 10–11 and expands Table 1. Existing principal plots and result tables are retained, with layout and placement adjustments.

improvement.justification: Human checks of instruction quality and safety judges address validation gaps in v1, while access information and new diagnostics improve usability and auditability. However, F.4 describes joint transition percentages as conditional rates, and F.5 overgeneralizes GPT-4.1's safety advantage: with single-turn memes, Table 14 reports HR 10.58% for GPT-4.1 versus 3.26% for GPT-4o. These interpretive problems limit the net quality gain.
